segments.text: In my town, when you turn 13, you spend one night alone in the woods, and what comes back is never quite you.
You walk in at sunset with one lantern, you walk out at sunrise, and every grown-up tells you the same rule.
Never let your lantern go out.
Everybody comes back. Same face, same clothes, same name.
But something's off. They don't blink as much, they laugh a second too late, and they never talk about what happened in the woods.
The parents throw a party anyway. Cake, balloons, welcome back!
But the kids whisper one word behind their backs. Swapped.
My big brother Jack went in last year. He came back smiling, but he didn't remember our treehouse,
the one with both our names carved in the door. And some nights, at three in the morning,
he'd stand in my doorway, just standing there, humming. My best friend Maya was two months older
than me, so she went in first. The night before, we made a pact. We picked a secret word, something
stupid. Thunderbird. If you come back and you don't know the word, it's not you. At sunrise,
I was waiting at the edge of the woods. She walked out, muddy, shaking. I grabbed her shoulders.
What's the word? One second, two. Then she smiled. Thunderbird. I almost cried. She was back. Over
Over the next weeks, she still laughed at my jokes.
Once, she laughed a second too late.
Only once.
The night before my birthday, Maya grabbed my hands.
Her hands were cold.
Eli, listen.
The lantern is how they find you.
Light pulls them in like moths.
Blow it out.
Hide in the dark.
That's how I made it.
Every grown-up said, never let it go out.
But Maya was my best friend.
At sunset, I walked into the woods.
My lantern swung, the only light for miles.
Then I heard footsteps all around me, matching mine, step for step.
I took a breath and blew out the lantern.
For one second, nothing.
Then, in the dark, two little lights opened.

eyes, pale and glowing, then two more, then ten, then a hundred, between every tree, all at my height, all watching me, a beam of moonlight came down through the branches, and something stepped into it, a kid, my size, my clothes, but where its face should be, there was nothing, smooth, blank, then its face started to change, a mouth, my mouth, my eyes, it smiled my smile and whispered, in my voice, thunderbird, I turned to run, hands grabbed my arms out of the dark, they pushed me against a tree, the bark was soft, like mud, it started to close over my wrists, then the moonlight spread across the clearing, and I saw them,
Faces in every tree, pressed into the bark.
Hundreds of kids, eyes open, mouths moving, no sound.
In the tree beside mine was Jack, my real brother, crying.
And on my other side was Maya, my real Maya.
Her mouth shaped one word over and over.
Run.
She never came back.
The girl who walked out knew our word because she pulled it right out of Maya's head.
And the lantern advice?
That was so they could take me.
The bar closed over my chest, my neck.
Through the trees, I saw the sun coming up.
And walking out toward town, muddy and smiling, was me.
Mom ran across the field and hugged him.
Maya was waiting.
What's the word?
He smiled.
